segments.text: That sensor can't see him. It's pointed at a plain, blank wall.
Yet researchers have used light bouncing off a wall to track someone hidden around a corner.
That dot is their position estimate. Not a photograph.
The trick is timing: light that reaches him takes the long way round, so it comes back later.
A few billionths of a second later.
This takes a time-of-flight sensor, a camera that clocks its own light's round trip.
So how do you turn a tiny delay into a location?
First, a puzzle: why does a plain wall work at all?
Put a mirror here, and our friend is simply visible.
A painted wall is rough up close. It throws light every which way, so each spot acts less like a mirror, more like a tiny lamp.
Everything coming back is a blend of many paths. What survives is timing.
Nearly everything coming back bounced once, off the wall. Our friend's echo bounced three times, so it's tiny.

This is real data from the same team, with a different sensor and hidden object: the wall's big echo, then, a few nanoseconds later, a bump you have to zoom in to see. In this capture, hundreds of times weaker.
That bump is the clue. Its timing says how much farther the light travelled.
Farther from where? Simplify it: the sensor flashes and listens at one spot on the wall.
Light covers about thirty centimetres every nanosecond. But the detour is there and back, so each extra nanosecond puts him only about fifteen centimetres farther from the wall spot.
Measure the extra delay, and you know how far he is from that spot. Not which direction. Just how far.
He could be anywhere on this arc, all the same distance from that spot.
Now listen at a second spot. Another delay, another arc. On this side of the wall, they cross in just one place.
Measured timings are a bit fuzzy, so each arc is really a band, and the bands overlap in a small patch.
These two spots are close, so the patch is long and blurry. Spread them out, and it shrinks.
In practice, a computer weighs many spots at once, trying positions and keeping those whose predicted echoes match. It also leans on assumptions, like what kind of object it's after.
That's why the answer is a likely location, or a rough shape.
And here's a real one.
Moved through known positions, the sensor behind that faint bump rebuilt the rough outline of a hidden U.
In 2012, an MIT team rebuilt the rough 3D shape of a hidden mannequin. By 2021, others had live video around corners.
But those ran on research equipment. One team had even tracked hidden objects with a cheap sensor.
Then, in a study published in 2026, a team from MIT and Dartmouth tried the small time-of-flight sensors, often called LiDAR, found in phones and gadgets.
Don't expect your phone to do this yet: phone makers often keep the raw data private.
Their new idea: a model that keeps track of what moved, so many weak frames can be combined.
Why would a smaller, cheaper sensor need that?
Weak lasers mean fainter echoes. The team's smartphone-grade device had about a hundred pixels: a hundred listening spots. And if you hold one in your hand, it jiggles.
Their fix borrows night mode's trick from phone cameras: stack many quick, dim frames into one better estimate.
The catch: things move between frames. He steps, and his echo shifts in time. The sensor jiggles, and its listening spots land somewhere new.
Just add them up, and echoes from different places blur into one smear, like a long exposure of someone walking.
So their model solves for one unknown at a time.
To build a shape, hold the object still and step the sensor through known positions, spreading out its listening spots. That's how the U was made.
To follow a person, hold the sensor still, and let each guess drift a little between frames, keeping the ones that still match. The estimate keeps up instead of smearing.
So what can it actually do, and where does it fail?
Take our opening clip: an off-the-shelf kit the authors put at under a hundred dollars, held still while a person walked behind a partition.
Many of their tests had help: safety-vest style reflective material on the target, which sends far more light straight back.
Our clip's files don't say if the walker wore any.
But in a separate test, the authors report tracking a person in ordinary clothes, capturing thirty frames a second.
What might this be good for? Picture a delivery robot nearing a blind warehouse corner.
With a suitable wall at the junction, a sensor like this might give it an early hint of movement out of sight.
Just a fuzzy blob: enough to say slow down, not enough to say who's there.
And plenty is still hard: short range, dark or shiny walls, bright sunlight, and fast math on small hardware. The researchers call it an early-stage prototype.
For now, it's a promising clue, not a safety system.
Being out of sight isn't the same as giving nothing away.
To really hide, he'd have to block the bounces too.
This is Future Got Weird: the strange future, explained. Subscribe for more, and we'll see you around the corner.
